AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES FOR ORPHANS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-117, to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act.
speakername: Mr, Joseph P. O'Keefe (Si. John's East) moved

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES FOR ORPHANS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES FOR ORPHANS
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to widen the discretion of the merchant seamen's compensation board so an allowance could be made to a person who undertook the care and maintenance of orphans of merchant seamen entitled to compensation under the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act.
Under the present wording of the act the allowance is payable only if the person concerned moves into the house of the deceased seaman's widow. This bill would permit an allowance to be paid at the discretion of the board when the orphans are cared for and maintained elsewhere than in the former household in a manner satisfactory to the board.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

May 24, 1967

subtopic: INABILITY OF MEMBERS TO ENTER CENTRE BLOCK

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INABILITY OF MEMBERS TO ENTER CENTRE BLOCK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is more properly one of privilege. Although the time now is past three o'clock, a number of members of this house have been unable to get into the house because the doors of the centre block are locked at the back, the side and the front. I should like to ask the minister responsible for the policing of this place to at least make it possible for members of parliament to be in their places when the bell is rung.

The house resumed from Tuesday, May 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp for committee of supply, and the amendment of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Lewis.

Mr. Speaker, when speaking in this debate just before the house adjourned last night I had been dealing with the crisis in the Near East and had noted the fact that the precipitate order for the withdrawal of the UN force in the Gaza strip had severely injured the prestige of the UN and thereby decreased its ability to act as an effective instrument for the preservation or restoration of peace. I also noted that in my view it was essential that steps be taken, both in the short run and the long run, to restore and enlarge this prestige.
I had been dealing with the situation which had developed between Israel and its Arab neighbours. Since that time we have learned that the Soviet union has made quite a strong statement in effect supporting the Arab states, and the U.S. president, President Johnson, also made a strong statement in effect supporting the position of Israel, particularly in so far as its right to use the gulf of Aqaba and have free passage for its ships through there is concerned.
The threat of war breaking out between Israel and its Arab neighbours of course created a very dangerous situation and, as I noted yesterday, one which because of the geographical position of that area and the alliances involved could very readily spread and become a world conflict. The present threat of direct intervention by the Russians on one side and the Americans on the other
Foreign Policy
creates a situation which could and would be catastrophic, I think. Certainly I would hope that in the UN security council, which has been meeting this morning and is to meet aga n this afternoon, it will be possible to arrive at a meeting of minds between the Russians on the one hand and the Americans and the western countries on the other hand with regard to preventing the threatened conflagration and leading to an agreement between these two super powers, Russia and the U.S., that they will not engage their own forces directly on one side or the other.
The threat of involvement by these two nations, particularly the active involvement of the U.S. in a fighting role, is of course something which I think all the western world must look upon as extremely serious from their own point of view, especially as at the present time the United States has committed such a large proportion of its forces to the Far East that its active involvement in the crisis in the Middle East would I think create an extraordinarily difficult and awkward situation for all the western countries, and a very dangerous one for the whole world. It seems to me that the UN security council, of which both these countries are members, is the place where some agreement to contain this war should be reached, and particularly to ensure that neither of these great powers becomes involved in it in a fighting way.
We also learned last night, through the papers at least, that in order to enforce the blockade of the gulf of Aqaba which had been declared the U.A.R. had already sown mines, and it had been intimated that they had taken other measures to ensure that Israeli ships or ships carrying strategic materials to the Israeli port of Eilath would not be allowed to pass through. Of course this creates a situation where any attempt on the part of an Israeli ship to go through that gulf is very likely to start a shooting war. Under these circumstances I would hope very much that the state of Israel would not attempt to force or break this blockade immediately. There is no doubt that what is required at the present is time to try to get this matter resolved and a peaceful settlement made. Therefore I hope the Canadian government and other governments will exert what pressure they can on Israel not to try to force this issue immediately, because of the very grave threat such action would carry of the outbreak of a general conflagration in that area.

Foreign Policy

May 24. 1967
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Last night I started to say something about the long term measures, which I think are essential, which the UN and its member countries should take in order to make it a more effective peace keeping organization and restore its prestige. The first one I noted was that it must work to get rid of some of the basic causes of conflict that I mentioned, particularly the existence of more than a million Palestinian refugees who are in the Gaza Strip, Jordan, Syria and Lebanon. There refugees constitute a possible source of fighting and difficulty between the Arab countries and the state of Israel. This is only one of what I might term the basic possible causes of conflict and one of the things which could produce a situation likely to lead to war.
I believe the United Nations must be much more active in attempting to resolve this problem which has been in existence since 1956. The United Nations has really done nothing more than feed these people on a semi-starvation diet. This is not good enough. I believe that until these people are dispersed by means of emigration to other countries, by absorption into the Arab countries or the return of some of them to Israel, the extremely strong feelings of hatred which exist throughout these areas will continue and will be reinforced by the existence of these refugee camps.
Another of the steps that the United Nations must take in order to make it possible for that body to carry effectively on peace keeping activities and the solving of problems such as the one to which I have been referring is the settlement of the payment of the costs of activities along this line as well as the general costs of the United Nations. One of the reasons the United Nations has not been able to play nearly as effective a part as it could is the fact it has not been in a position to deal with the basic problem of finding the funds for these operations.
In so far as peace keeping operations are concerned, we know that certain countries have refused to pay their share of the costs. This is a problem the United Nations has always tended to avoid and has refused to have a showdown with regard to it. Although the United States is the subject of condemnation in many parts of the world, as well as in the United States and Canada, had it not been for the regular and special contributions made by that country the United Nations likely would have gone bankrupt and probably ceased to exist quite some time ago. This

is not a problem which can continue to be swept under the rug. Something must be done about it if the United Nations is to be effective.
A third step which I think needs to be taken is to introduce a more effective voting procedure at the United Nations. As long as we have a situation in which a country like Cyprus with about half a million people and other countries with an even smaller number of people have the same vote as a country such as the U.S.S.R. with 200 million people and the United States with some 200 million or India with several hundred million, we have a completely unrealistic situation. I do not believe the United Nations can operate effectively in such a situation. There must be, therefore, a change in the voting procedure. There must be a weighted system of voting introduced into this body if it is going to continue to get support from the larger and more important nations. This is absolutely essential if the organization is to operate effectively.
I should like to say something about the withdrawal plans so far as the United Nations emergency force in the Gaza Strip is concerned. I must protest the fact that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) yesterday refused to give us any information whatever when questioned in the house with regard to these plans. However, he then made a television appearance last night and gave a considerable amount of information. He has to some extent repeated today in answer to questions what he said on television but has refused to give any further information. On the basis of past experience I expect he will be appearing on television again to announce what is going to be done. This is a direct affront to the House of Commons. In view of the situation existing in the world today, I do not wish to introduce any partisan bickering or anything along those lines, but certainly information of this kind should be given in the House of Commons, not refused here and then given over television. I hope that the proper course will be followed in the future.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I should like to point out to the Minister of National Defence and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that there is a very natural concern on the part of all Canadians with regard to the situation of our troops in the Gaza Strip and what arrangements have been made to get them out, particularly if a conflagration should start there. This concern is felt particularly, of course, by the relatives of
May 24, 1967

these people, some of whom I know are extremely anxious. Therefore I believe it is the responsibility of the government to make public its plans for the withdrawal of our troops from the Gaza Strip. I do not believe it is good enough for the Minister of National Defence to say he does not think it would be wise to release the contingency plans. The point is there are several thousand relatives of the men who are stationed there who are very anxious about the situation and they have a right to know what arrangements have been made for the withdrawal of these men. In addition to the people directly concerned, to a lesser extent all Canadians are concerned. I understand the Prime Minister is going to speak later today, so I hope he will give some information about this matter and allay some of the fears which exist amongst the relatives of these men.
I do not know just what the minister meant by the statement he made on television last night that the contingency plans involve possible withdrawal by sea, by land and by air. Having been in that part of the world and spent some time there in the Rafa camp and at El Arish, I know there are only three ways in which troops can be withdrawn from there. The first means is by air from El Arish airfield, the only available airfield. The second means is by sea by very light draft vessels because only such vessels can get into the small fishing port of Gaza. The third means would be by road to Suez and Cairo. Another possible alternative, I suppose, would be by reopening the road from the Gaza Strip into Israel, but I do not believe that is a practical proposition with the two sides facing each other there.
These are the only ways in which you can get people out of the Gaza Strip. What arrangements may have been made with the Egyptians concerning the withdrawal of people by road to Suez and Cairo airport I do not know, but we should be given information. The answer the minister gave yesterday left the situation concerning the use of the El Arish airfield very much in doubt. From his answer I do not know whether we could still use that airfield. The minister said that he did not know whether the last Canadian aircraft had left there. If that airfield is not available we shall be reduced to two means of evacuation from that area.
Before finishing I wish to say something briefly about Viet Nam. On the face of it the N.D.P. amendment looks innocuous but I do
Foreign Policy
not think there is any question that the intention-and it should be taken this way-is to condemn the United States presence in Viet Nam and condemn the United States bombing of Viet Nam. The amendment calls on the United States to withdraw unilaterally from that activity.
I do not think that the passage of such an amendment in this house would do any good and it might do considerable harm. First, it would do no good because it would have no effect on the policy which the United States government might follow. Second, it might cause considerable resentment on the part of some members of the United States government and it might make it more difficult for us to exert useful pressure on that government. Third, such a motion would aid and comfort the government of North Viet Nam and the Viet Cong, leading them to believe that the United States will be forced to succumb to pressure to stop the bombing and to withdraw.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
In just a moment. In my view the passage of such an amendment would more likely prolong the unfortunate situation in Viet Nam than end it. Would the hon. member ask his question now?

Would the hon. member not wish to comment on what the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said during this debate, that we should ask for the bombing to cease. Does the hon. member not think that that request, too, would have the ill effects of which he has spoken as the consequence of passing the subamendment?

My personal view is that the cessation of bombing should go hand in hand with the withdrawal of North Vietnamese troops from South Viet Nam. That should be done as a matter of agreement. If anything like that could be accomplished we should all be in favour of it. I do not think that a demand on the United States unilaterally to withdraw its troops would serve the cause of peace. I disagree with any such resolution.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

In just a moment. Many who violently condemn the United States action and presence in Viet Nam presume that the United States is there because of selfish, immoral or imperialistic purposes, and on that

May 24. 1967
Foreign Policy
basis they condemn not only the United States presence but everything she does. In my view there is no basis for this attitude. The United States is trying to preserve democratic government in South Viet Nam and has no selfish interests, apart from her interest in containing the general spread of communism. Those who condemn the United States in such strong terms never mention that she was asked by the South Vietnamese government to assist in the struggle against the Viet Cong and North Viet Nam.
I was glad to see that yesterday the hon. member for Greenwood did not presume that the United States was in Viet Nam for selfish, immoral or imperialistic purposes. He gave the United States credit for good intentions but said he believed the United States was following a course which would lead to disaster. There were, he said, differences of opinion. This, I think, is correct. Every party in the house harbours persons with different opinions about the situation in Viet Nam and about the best course to be followed. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) showed by his speech that he has his own opinion. These are all honest differences. But I do not think that those who believe that immediately the United States stops the bombing the problem in Viet Nam will be solved have any more information to rely on than have others who think differently.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
As soon as I have finished I shall be glad to answer the question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Calgary North has the floor.

Those who believe that ending the bombing will immediately solve the problem have no more information to rely on or basis for their belief than have those who believe the opposite. I am certain that those advocating such a cessation have far less background information for their opinions than has the United States government which also has a responsibility in this matter. The United States is the supreme power in the western world and it is responsible for maintaining peace and containing communism. That being so, one ought to give the United States government credit for following its policies. Many think those policies are wrong. Personally I do not concur with everything the United States has done in Viet Nam and elsewhere. On the other hand, condemning the IMr. Harkness.)
United States generally is neither a reasonable nor an effective way of restoring or maintaining peace. I would be glad to answer the hon. member's question.

I wonder whether the hon. gentleman could tell us, from what he knows and from what he has studied, whether the United States bombing has increased or decreased the flow of troops from North Viet Nam to South Viet Nam?
It is apparent, I think, that I have no direct knowledge in this regard. My general information is that the bombing has cut down what would have been a much larger flow of troops and supplies.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has now expired.
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Before the Prime Minister takes the floor I understand that the Leader of the Opposition wishes to raise a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, the question of privilege must be raised at once. I am sorry that I have to come before the Prime Minister at this time but what I wish to say has to do with the conduct that was referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. This afternoon the doors of the parliament building were locked and the hon. member had to find his way in by indirect means. At 3.05 this afternoon the front and west doors were still locked, with the front doors being guarded by the R.C.M.P.
There is a long line-up of farmers outside the front door and it is strange they should be treated as though they were lawless individuals who endanger parliament. They have a right of public protest. Parl'ament does not belong to the government. After four years of indifference to the farmers this government closes them out.

Oh, oh.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
It closes them out from parliament. These are not agitators. They are not lawless. They are entitled to be treated like other Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you will wish to look into this question which was raised earlier this afternoon, as a matter of fact, by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton).
May 24. 1967

I am privileged to participate in this debate after the very thoughtful contribution which has just been made by the hon. gentleman who preceded me. My first remarks will be directed to the subject of Viet Nam, the tragedy of Viet Nam, because by implication it is the subject of the amendment and, explicitly, the subject of the subamendment.
In moving the subamendment the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said he thought the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) must have had a sense of humour to have introduced his amendment and then suggested it did not involve the matter of confidence. Obviously it is a reflection on the government and a criticism of the policy of the government. The hon. member for York South must have exactly the same sense of humour, because the subamendment he introduced is of precisely the same character. It represents a vote of non-confidence in the policy of the government on a matter of very great importance indeed. We do not propose at this time to accept this subamendment because it represents, as the hon. gentleman who has just preceded me pointed out, a onesided approach to this problem. It deals with one aspect alone of that problem, though I agree it is an important one.
The view behind the subamendment is that we are not dealing with a case of aggression from the north, that in Viet Nam, as the hon. member put it yesterday, there is merely a civil war and that the United States had no right to be there from the beginning. In the hon. member's words-I took them from Hansard because I did not have the pleasure of hearing the whole of his interesting speech- "the world's mightiest power has intervened in a local situation". He went on to point out that Hanoi, on the other hand, had limited its activities in Viet Nam and had bombed nobody. On the basis of this statement and others he made he adjures us as follows: "Let us recognize these facts. What right has the United States to be there in that situation?" This, I believe, is the basis of his approach, and the approach of those who feel as he does.
I believe that the purposes and objectives of United States policy in Viet Nam were not aggression. I believe that the United States moved into Viet Nam in the first place to help South Viet Nam, at the invitation of the government of that country, to defend itself against military action and subversive terrorism aimed at preventing the people of that part of Viet Nam making their own decision
Foreign Policy
as to their future development and political institutions rather than having one particular solution forced upon them under the guise of a liberation struggle conducted in the interests of a totalitarian communist regime in North Viet Nam which has not allowed and does not intend to allow its own people any choice as to their social, economic or political system.
Mr. Bundy, who played an important part in these matters in earlier days as adviser on foreign affairs to the president, has written these words:
United States policy remains based on the continuing conviction that we should be ready to do our full share to help prevent the communists from taking south Viet Nam by force and terror.
We may not agree with this policy, but I think those words are a rational explanation of the policy followed by men in the United States who are men of good will and as peace loving as we are. I can understand their position in this regard. That does not mean a government in Canada has to support or approve all the measures taken or all the measures adopted by the United States forces in Viet Nam, let alone by the governments in Saigon-and remember there have been more governments than one-in achieving their purposes. And on occasions when I have felt it necessary to speak publicly and not confine myself to diplomacy-I do not care very much for the phrase "quiet diplomacy"; if diplomacy is to be any good it is bound to be quiet-I have made this clear.
I have spoken publicly when I felt it was necessary to do so and might be of some value. Two years ago in Philadelphia I proposed a pause in the bombing for what I thought would be a helpful purpose, and later I think I was the only head of a western government who publicly regretted the resumption of bombing. I still regret it. I think it was a great mistake on the part of the United States administration at that time to resume the bombing in the circumstances in which it was resumed. But this does not mean and will not mean, in present circumstances at least, that we should join that chorus which has denounced the Untied States for being in Viet Nam at all. That is a different matter.
If this is our position I do not think we will accomplish anything constructive by accusing the United States of sole guilt and sole blame for what has happened in that country and by doing so try to impose a kind of moral sanction against the United States. It seems to me

May 24, 1967
Foreign Policy
that anyone in the position of governmental responsibility-and I am certainly in that position-who adopted those tactics would by doing so cut or certainly weaken the lines of official communication between Ottawa and Washington on this subject and I cannot think any useful purpose would be achieved by doing that, especially if we felt we could use those lines of communication to give good advice to our friends. Yet to accept this careful and constructive course and reject more exciting courses of word and action means, obviously, that we will be sneered at by some who consider us to be a satellite or a lap-dog or some unpleasant animal because we are not willing to get up on a public platform and condemn the United States in a way which those who criticize us most harshly do not condemn the communist side.
Hear, hear.

Because we take this attitude we are accused of political immorality and of being faint-hearted in the cause of peace. I can accept that accusation with equanimity as long as I feel X am following the right course.

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

I wonder whether the
Prime Minister will allow me a question. I have to say in prelude to the question that I agree entirely it is not a one-way street and that the condemnation of the Americans as aggressors is entirely unjustified. But using that as a principle, can the Prime Minister not go along with the statement made yesterday by His Holiness the Pope calling for an end to the bombing by the United States, fortifying as it did U Thant's statement that a continuation would be dangerous to world peace?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I go along 100 per cent with the statement made by His Holiness the Pope yesterday, because it is a statement which has been made on this side in the House of Commons, and outside it, when we previously advocated bringing an end to the bombing and, associated with that, an end to the infiltration of troops from the north into the south.
Hear, hear.

This is not a one-sided matter. There can be very honest, sincere, and indeed emotional differences of opinion on it. Last night I was looking over the record of the negotiation offers that had been made in the

last two or two and a half years, each one of which had been rejected by the government in Hanoi and accepted by the government in Washington. I am leaving out of these offers those made by the United States government itself.
These were offers made by the United Kingdom on February 20, 1965, by the 17 non-aligned nations on April 1, 1965, by the government of India, by the Prime Ministers of the Commonwealth-and I was one of them who initiated a plan for a special mission to visit the capitals of the countries involved to explore the circumstances in which a conference might be held to end the fighting, and which was rejected by Hanoi and by Peking-by the British foreign secretary's proposal made in Moscow on December 2, 1965, by the proposal made by Pope Paul VI on December 19, 1965, by the proposal made by the Secretary General in April, 1966 and again in August
1966,	when he first suggested his three-point plan as the basis for a negotiated settlement, including the cessation of the bombing of North Viet Nam, the scaling down of all military activities by all sides in Viet Nam, and the willingness to enter into discussions with those actually fighting; by the offer made by the Prime Minister of India on July 7, 1966, which was a detailed proposal for negotiations within the framework of the Geneva agreements and included a proposal to reconvene the Geneva conference.
Did I understand the Prime Minister to say Washington accepted U Thant's three-point proposal, including the cessation of bombing?

That is my information because the cessation of bombing was linked with the general talks, and that was repeated by the Secretary General later on December 30, 1966.
On October 24, 1966, the United Arab Republic, India and Yugoslavia issued a communique with a proposal for measures to bring about a negotiated settlement. On December 8, 1966 Pope Paul made another proposal. The British foreign secretary made one on December 30, 1966, as did the Secretary General again on that day; and on March 14,
1967,	the Secretary General made a further proposal, as my hon. friend knows, providing for general talks preliminary to the reconvening of the Geneva conference. In addition there were the two temporary cessations of bombing by the United States, but in all these cases where these proposals were made, and I repeat they were not made by Americans, they were not acceptable to the government
May 24, 1967

in Hanoi. This does not mean that we should not try to find some proposal that is acceptable to all parties, and of course we will continue to strive to do that.
The other day I read an editorial in a very influential Washington newspaper, the Washington Star. I believe it was in the edition of May 18, and I would like to quote one or two paragraphs from that editorial. The editor of the Washington Star says:
The time has come in the Star's opinion for the U.S.A. to stop bombing in North Viet Nam. We say this without the slightest apology for the administration's conduct of the war up to now. The decision to start bombing was necessary and right. An aggressor cannot be permitted to take for granted his security at home while he wages war on his neighbours. The policy of the careful escalation of bombing subject to tight restrictions on the choice of targets seemed likely to bring Hanoi to its senses and has had our full support.
But-
The editorial goes on:
-every military strategy must be subject to constant review and reappraisal. It is necessary to weigh the gains against the risks, to ask whether hoped-for results are in fact being achieved. It is necessary to watch for the moment where a change of strategy may produce a greater gain at a decreased risk. That moment has arrived. We should say nothing, explain nothing, set no conditions or limitations on our switch of strategy. We should simply stop bombing and see what the enemy does.
Hear, hear.
This is a position taken by one American newspaper, and it is a position taken by a great many Americans-
The New York Times is the same.

-including most recently a very prominent United States senator. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the administration in Washington is giving very careful consideration to this idea which has been repeated in recent weeks by many inside the United States.
I do not think, however, that the adoption of the subamendment by this house, by a parliament outside the United States, would serve the purpose that we have in mind of bringing this war to an end. It is a type of amendment which has not been dealt with by any other parliament friendly to the United States that I know of, and I do not think this kind of amendment would serve the purpose we have in mind.
Hear, hear.

Indeed, if we begin to give this kind of formal parliamentary advice
Foreign Policy
from outside the United States it might conceivably have the opposite effect. I also think, Mr. Speaker, we should be careful not to put our hopes so high in regard to the abandonment of the bombing of North Viet Nam that we are likely to run into disillusionment if that should take place and fail. I myself would not attach excessive expectations to peace and a negotiated settlement if the bombing should end tomorrow.
We might as we have in the past-by "we" I mean the western countries, the friends of the United States-well run up against what has been encountered before, namely, escalation of demand on the other side. So I think it might be desirable to find out what the reaction in Hanoi would be to an immediate and unconditional end to the bombing of the north. Would they stop fighting and begin talking and, if they refused or attached a new condition, would the danger of massive escalation be increased? This is another factor we have to take into consideration. These are the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why we on this side of the house cannot support the subamendment which is, of course, a motion of no confidence in the government.
Now I want to come to the other matter which has been engaging us, and rightly so, in this debate-the situation in the Middle East, in Palestine, the seriousness of which certainly cannot be exaggerated. As my right hon. friend said yesterday, and I am paraphrasing his words, it is hard to imagine getting closer to catastrophe than in the way we seem to have been drifting in the last day or two. I, as have other members of the house, have had some connection with this situation for a good many years, in fact since I first went down to the United Nations at the end of the war when the state of Palestine was established by United Nations action.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The basic issue in this situation it seems to me, as has already been mentioned in this debate, is the recognition of Israel's right to live in peace and security. The rejection and repudiation of that basic right has been over the years and is now a source of our danger. It is not the immediate manifestation of that danger but it certainly is a source of it. So long as Israel's neighbours, or some of them, refuse to recognize the right of Israel to exist as a state, then we move from one crisis to another. We already have moved from one to another over the last 10 or 15 years. Israel, of course, also has the basic obligation, which I

May 24, 1967
Foreign Policy
am sure she accepts, to live without provocation and threat to her neighbours and in accord with the United Nations decisions which gave her birth. This is the continuing issue.
There is, however, an immediate crisis arising fundamentally out of this issue which now threatens war. I am perhaps repeating the obvious but the danger point it seems to me, and perhaps the most dangerous point, is the situation in Sharm el Sheikh. The troops of the United Arab Republic now control this port in the Gulf of Aqaba. In 1957 we spent days and nights arguing about this particular aspect of the settlement which it was hoped would have been reached at least in accord with the withdrawal of the Israeli troops from the ground they had conquered. They made it quite clear at that time that they visualized a package deal by which, in return for withdrawing from vital strategic points, and especially from Sharm el Sheikh, they would be protected against action from those areas, and particularly this point, which would prejudice and destroy their own national interest. They undoubtedly feel they have a commitment to that effect.
We need not go into the legal situation. Perhaps it should be sent to the international Court of Justice for judgment, but before the International Court of Justice could render a judgment many things would have to be done to avoid trouble because the Gulf of Aqaba now is of vital importance to the existence of the state of Israel. From 90 to 92 per cent of her oil goes past the strait of Tiran and into the gulf to the port of Elath. That certainly is one very dangerous point.
The second dangerous point is the Gaza Strip which now has been taken over by what is called the Palestine Liberation Army, a part of the force of the United Arab Republic. This army is composed of men devoted, and fanatically and sincerely devoted, to what they believe to be the liberation of their homeland. They are there now in the Gaza strip with 300,000 Palestinian refugees. If there could be a more explosive situation than that, I do not know what it could be.
The third point is the Syrian border which has been the scene of terrorist incidents and activities in recent weeks and which perhaps has been the occasion for the development of the recent crisis, which can explode at any minute. The fourth danger point is the possibility of excessive reaction or retaliation by land, water or air against provocations or terrorist incidents.
The feeling of some of the people on the spot is, "Let's force this issue and have it over." That can be just as dangerous as the development of the other three points I have mentioned-the temptation, if you like, to pre-emptive a war. There is another danger, the danger of expanding this conflict if it takes place and if the United Nations is not able to limit it as it was earlier. There is the danger of the United States lining up behind one party and the U.S.S.R. lining up behind the other party. I cannot imagine a more frightening danger than that because, without the United Nations intervention, that could turn what might be a local conflict into a global tragedy.
Behind all the dangers we notice now, from press, radio and television reports, the danger of inflammatory statements and attitudes- the war of the air waves, the demonstrations, people marching down the street shouting, "We want war". These are the poor deluded people who would be the first to suffer from war. A leader in that part of the world is reported as having said the day before yesterday, "They threaten us with war; our answer is, we welcome war".
All this adds up to a terrifying situation. So what do we do about it? We all have our responsibilities as members of the United Nations. We have decided, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) mentioned yesterday, that we will try to discharge our responsibility by getting this matter before the security council of the United Nations as quickly as possible. Yesterday the members of the council from Canada and Denmark asked for the convening of the security council. That meeting is taking place today.
Whenever this world gets into trouble, where does it go? It goes to the United Nations. The worse the trouble, the more important the United Nations becomes and as soon as the trouble is settled or put aside for the time being by the United Nations, it is then forgotten and everybody falls back on their own nationalist pride, privileges, fears and hatreds. But at the moment we all say, "Let the United Nations take over". I do not know of anything else which could do it better, unless we had a conference of the four great powers. If they could work together, that would be equally effective and more effective if they worked through the security council in doing it.

May 24. 1967

Our ambassador to the United Nations in dealing with this matter this morning had this to say:
In calling this Security Council meeting we are suggesting that council should exercise its responsibilities under the charter to deal with the kind of threatening situation which the Secretary General has not only reported to the Security Council, but has regarded as sufficiently serious to assume the responsibility for undertaking a personal mission to the area.
The situation as the Secretary General rightly reported to the council has shown signs of "increasingly dangerous deterioration" for some time.
Tension also grew as a result of terroristic and sabotage activities on the borders of Israel and Syria and the Secretary General reported that the functions and resources of UNTSO had not enabled that organization to arrest these activities.
In recent days there have been statements by the President of the U.A.R. and the Prime Minister of Israel which face us with the danger of direct confrontation between the U.A.R. and Israel over the question of access to the Gulf of Aqaba.
In face of this rising and dangerous state of tension means of bringing influences of moderation to bear in areas through U.N. far from having been increased have been decreased at the very moment of crisis by withdrawal of UNEF.
The principal means to balance this deteriorating situation through the U.N. has been the mission of the Secretary General himself.
I believe at this stage the most useful contribution which this council can make to this grave situation is to reinforce the current efforts being made by the Secretary General to preserve peace in the area. This is the purpose of what we are suggesting the council should do. We should at the same time urge that no member state of the U.N. take any action which would either prejudice the success of the Secretary General's mission or worsen the situation.
In the face of grave facts, in the face of the mounting threat and fait accompli, how can the international community discharge its collective duty unless the moral influence of the Security Council, which is charged under Article 24 of the charter with primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security precisely "to ensure prompt and effective action"-and I underline these words-is brought to bear upon the seriously deteriorating situation in the Middle East?
This, in sum, is the aim of our initiative. Canada is a friend of all the nations of the area and has always striven to help by whatever means we can to maintain peace and stability in the area, and to assist those in trouble and distress. What we now ask is that the Security Council, and in particular all of its permanent members who bear special responsibility, add the weight of its influence collectively by asking that no member of the United Nations take any action which would worsen the situation and to jeopardize the efforts of the Secretary General to preserve the peace. This is what we ask the Security Council to do at this stage; we believe it can do no less.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I hope that in due course it will be able to do more. Certainly at the present time the
Foreign Policy
important thing is to do nothing to exacerbate the situation, and that applies, as my right hon. triend suggests, to the government of Israel which should be very careful about unnecessarily running any so called blockade if that would provoke the kind of retaliation which might have overriding results.

Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister allow a question? In view of the admonition uttered by the representative of Canada at the security council yesterday, is it a fact that the United States, through its ambassador designate Richard Nolte, advised the Egyptian foreign minister Mohammed Riad that Egypt should be warned that the United States will use force if necessary to hold open the Gulf of Aqaba for Israeli shipping, or is that statement merely one of speculation?

I cannot confirm that, and so far as I am concerned it is speculation. At this time only the United States could confirm the authenticity or otherwise of that story. I know that individual governments feel that they have their own special responsibilities and commitments, but I would hope that all these will be made secondary to the greatest commitment of all today, their duty as members of the United Nations security council. This will, of course, require moderation, tolerance and patience on the part of everybody concerned.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that each of the five major powers has the power of veto, has there been any indication that the U.S.S.R. is viewing this matter through the eyes of the Prime Minister in the way he has indicated in his statements today?

I certainly hope that to be the case and that they will work with the other permanent members of the security council. As my right hon. friend knows, there has already been a proposal made that these powers meet as a committee, and it would be very helpful if that could be done. As soon as that meeting takes place I hope it will be possible to bring other activities within the ambit of the United Nations security council.
Having regard to the situation that we face in the security council, our ambassador and the ambassador of Denmark have moved or are about to move in the security council in New York the following proposal, that the security council, having been seized with the current situation in the Middle East, express

May 24, 1967
Foreign Policy
full support for the efforts of the Secretary General to pacify the situation and request all states to refrain from any step which might worsen the situation, and invite the Secretary General to report to the security council upon his return so that the security council may *continue its consideration of the matter. I hope a resolution of this kind will be accepted by the members of the security council and that it will at least hold the line for the time being. Nothing can be more important than that. There will have to be subsequent steps, but I often wonder why, as the result of these critical situations in respect of which we find ways and means of avoiding open conflict, we cannot go one step forward and find a continuing solution to those things which brought about the conflict in the first place. That is something for the future.
There are things which we can do in the United Nations in the immediate future. This has been a great blow in one sense to our peace keeping ideas and hopes. However, peace keeping itself becomes more important than ever in the light of what has happened in the last three or four days. If the United Nations emergency force had not been withdrawn this situation might not have developed. The lesson to be learned from that is that when we send these United Nations peace keeping forces into these difficult areas we must do our best to make sure they have the foundation on which to act and that their work cannot be sabotaged except on order from the United Nations agency which sent them there.
This did not happen in respect of this United Nations emergency force. I remember very well the background, and I am not being critical of the Secretary General because I have no doubt that on an examination of the documents one would come to the conclusion that what he did was right in terms of the documentary evidence. There was a special arrangement made between Mr. Ham-marskjold and President Nasser. I objected to that arrangement at the time because I thought it might cause a lot of trouble in the future.
At that time we did not follow this preferable course because we had to get these people over there quickly in view of the fact the war was going on, and if by this kind of an agreement, very fuzzy in its language-Mr. Hammarskjold was a past master in this regard-the U.A.R. would accept this force, we thought we had better not go into the legalistic details too closely but get our troops on the spot.

This force was there for over ten years under this arrangement. This situation does not apply to Cyprus because we have a security council resolution as a basis for authority in that regard. What we have to do now is not weaken in our pursuit of peace keeping under the United Nations but strengthen our activities to obtain better peace keeping arrangements. I do not think there is any possibility of reviving this United Nations emergency force which certainly served gallantly for ten and a half years and has earned the gratitude of all the nations of the world. All the Canadians in that force have earned our gratitude over the last ten and a half years.
There is United Nations machinery available, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs said yesterday, including the United Nations truce supervisory organization and the four mixed armistice commissions, three of which are operating on the borders of Jordan and Lebanon and in Cyprus. The fourth has not been operating in respect of the United Arab Republic partly because it was not needed so much there in that the UNEF was located there, and partly because the Israeli government did not recognize its activities.
We can use this machinery in the hope that we can get the United Nations presence back into that area. What we and all the peace loving governments must do today is try to keep that blue flag flying between possible combatants. If we can do that we will have accomplished a great deal, even though the force may not be armed with the heaviest and most modern weapons available. 1 am not sure this would preserve the peace in the present circumstances but I think it would help, and I hope the security council will be able to take this first step by passing this first resolution. We are not sure of that but we hope we will be able to move further and at least consider this United Nations machinery which will do this job in perhaps a different way, by patrolling the boundaries and keeping the combatants from fighting each other.
In the meantime we are facing a dangerous and critical situation from hour to hour and we can only hope that no one in any country directly concerned, irrespective of the emotions of the moment or what might seem to be the possibility of emotion, will do anything or say anything which will start off what is bound to be a bloody war in that area and what might be a bloody war in a much greater area.
May 24, 1967
Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister answer a question? Is he prepared to say something now about the plans for the withdrawal of our Canadian troops in the Gaza Strip?

I have discussed this matter with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) who yesterday mentioned two sets of plans. There is the United Nations plan, which is a very carefully prepared plan for the evacuation of all members of the United Nations force. So far as we know, the United Nations authorities think that plan will be adequate, provided of course that the roof does not fall in.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This is the trouble.

That is the trouble, but they are very much aware of it and as a matter of urgency they are trying to bring their plans into line with that possibility. Meanwhile, as the Minister of National Defence has said, we have moved three ships in that direction and have worked out an emergency plan which we hope and believe will take care of our people. I hope that as soon as it is possible the Minister of National Defence will be able to give the house all the details in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Prime Minister would permit one brief question. Could he give us any idea, or does he have any suggestions, as to why the Egyptian government has taken this action at this particular time.

I have my own views that I would be very glad to discuss with my hon. friend, who I hope would be very interested in my views as I would be in his. But I do not think I should discuss them in public; they are just speculative on my part.

Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister answer a question before he sits down? Do I take it from the Prime Minister's remark that the position the Canadian representative on the security council will take is that all nations, including Israel, should have free access to the Gulf of Aqaba as an international water and that no nation, Egypt or any other, should have the right to blockade or block access to a free port?

We believe that under international law, and especially since the convention was passed in the United Nations in 1952, I think, or 1953, these are international waters and the ships of all nations have access
Division
to them and passage through them. There are a good many cases of international law dealing with this matter. This particular United Nations treaty, however, has not been signed by the U.A.R. and the government of the U.A.R. has not admitted the contention that they are international waters. But we certainly think so, as do most countries in the world.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is a period during which grievances may be expressed I would like to call attention to a subject which was raised earlier by the 23,000 farmers who have come to Parliament Hill. I believe this is an important matter and I was surprised to learn there is apparently considerable resentment on the part of the farmers as to the hearing they were given. I listened carefully to the remarks which were made by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauv6), who I felt was very rough with the people to whom he spoke. I also listened carefully to what was said by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene). To some extent I sympathize with one or two of the points he made.
When the Minister of Agriculture replied to the farmers' representations after considering the brief presented by their executive, he said
Problems of Farmers
he was often perturbed because representatives of some sections of the agricultural industry presented requests to parliament which were not necessarily in harmony with requests made by other segments of the industry. This is a legitimate point to make. It is my understanding that over the years it is not often a group of farmers has come to Ottawa pledged to seek a common goal which would result in a better deal for farmers as a whole.
I believe that the difficulties being encountered today by the dairy industry, though it is true they are in the forefront as a result of government policy, are only part of a larger problem which confronts our farmers, namely, that the prices they receive for the goods they sell are not enough to enable them to expand their enterprises and keep them up to date. The farmers to whom I spoke today were concerned not only with subsidies. They were concerned about the difficulty they encountered in raising sufficient money to turn their farms into economic units. They were concerned because the money they earned was insufficient to meet the costs of their operations.
Dairy farmers in my own area at the present time are having to spend from $500 to $1,500 on bulk coolers. This would represent a perfectly legitimate cost to the industry if the producers were receiving anything like the prices which consumers pay for their products. But this is not the case. Not long ago I was going over the books kept by my brother who runs a dairy farm in northern Ontario. He is a producer of fluid milk, selling about 70 per cent of his milk apart from his quota. Last year this milk went for manufacture and the government paid a subsidy in connection with it. This meant his price was somewhere in the five dollar range. This year the fluid milk price was $6.60 and the price of the milk sold for manufacture was $4.25, less delivery charges in each case. When the price was averaged out the milk was showing a return of approximately $4.50 or $4.60. The reason it is hard to calculate exactly is that there is a dairy requirement in the fluid milk quota which varies anywhere from 5 per cent to 15 per cent, and this is sold at a secondary price within the fluid milk market. This makes it difficult to calculate exactly what the total price is to the farmer.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
If the farmers in my area were able to get $6.60 per hundredweight there is no question

May 24, 1967
Problems of Farmers
that they would be able to afford the expansion which is necessary to retain the fluid milk market in the position it has occupied in the dairy industry. It would allow them to upgrade their milk, to put in bulk coolers and to handle their own depots if that is what they desire. The farmers in my area are good businessmen, and in the communities of New Liskeard, Haileybury and Cobalt they have their own dairy.
They found that in operating a fluid milk dairy in a fluid milk market they had to have the machinery to handle the secondary milk and the manufacturing milk. The farmers sold their manufacturing milk to the dairy, which established a quota. However, it was not long until this became a great cost to the dairy and the dairy fell weeks behind in its payments to the farmers. Before the farmers were able to arrange a sale of the dairy they themselves were carrying about a month's cost of the operation of the dairy in the form of non-payments from the dairy.
I raise this to point out that the problem is not only in the one field. It exists in a number of fields. When the farmer who is in the fluid milk field, receiving a fairly good price in that field, enters the manufacturing milk field a problem is immediately created. My brother is not a big farmer, but certainly the family "has been in the dairy industry for quite a number of years. He is running a very effective and efficient operation, and in the manufacturing field he has about the maximum quota available to the manufacturing producer. In other words, his surplus runs somewhere about 300,000 pounds per year in the manufacturing field.
He has admitted, and I am sure most other farmers would agree, that farmers would be much better off if the milk price were $5 and they d d not get the $6.60. If they could sell all their production at $5 the farmers would probably receive an increase in price of anywhere from 25 cents to 75 cents per hundredweight over what they are now getting on their total production.
The fact is that the federal government has got into the quota business in the manufacturing field. A producer of over 300,000 pounds is not a large producer. His stock would probably total about 25 cows, not a big dairy operation. Anything he had over that would be surplus to the manufacturing quota and would be sold on the market at $3.54.
Today the farmers are not only concerned about the dairy problem but about the overall farm problem as they see it. They are
[Mr. Peters.1
faced with a labour shortage. The cost of farm labour is very high. Farmers have received very little co-operation from the federal government to allow them to bring in people to work on their farms. However, there has been some immigration from places like Holland, and on occasion there has been migratory help from Mexico and other countries. In the main farm help has been accidentally secured and very temporary.
Many farmers get casual help off the street, workers who come in for a day and who want to get paid at the end of the day. After that the farmers do not see them again. Anyone who works on a farm knows that is not the kind of help that is required even in the emergency situation of harvesting production.
During the meeting in Ottawa today the farmers also talked about eggs, about the poultry problem and about potatoes. There were delegations present from New Brunswick. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island and from as far west as Alberta. The case they presented to the government is an industry problem. It is not confined to a specific part of farming but is a general farm problem.
The government has said that it is embarking on a program which will eliminate small farms and create economic units. It says that the farmers on these economic units will automatically be placed in a reasonable financial position. In my opinion this is not correct. It will again create a class of farmer who cannot make a living on the farm and we will reach a position where all farmers will be eliminated except those operating on large amalgamated or co-operative farms. This may be good enough in Russia, and it may be good enough for the Liberal party, but in my opinion it is not good enough for the members of the farm population of this nation who want to operate their own farms independently, with sufficient capital gain to take care of the expansion that is necessary and will continue to be necessary if they are to meet the commitments of the farm community toward the hungry people of our country.
I have suggested many times, although this is not accepted by the majority of farmers, that the only solution to the dairy problem will be the pooling of the total production of the dairy industry. The industry itself will have to be directed for the simple reason that the federal government will have to establish a marketing agency to dispose of dairy produce. The directing body will have to tell the manufacturing industry to produce skim milk
May 24, 1967

powder when it is needed for a certain market, and to manufacture cheese when it is specifically needed for another market. If that is done I believe that the people we have on the road selling farm produce will be able to compete in world markets and will be able to sell far more agricultural production than is now possible. The system we now have is creating shortages. We have cut off the small farmer, the guy who took a can of cream down to the dairy on the week end. We have cut off the man who had four or five cows and who wanted to get a farm but could not get a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation.
The Farm Credit Corporation will not lend money to someone who wants to enter farming. It will only lend to people who have so much collateral that they really do not need a loan from the corporation. We do not have the machinery to establish new farms. We do not assist the establishment of new farms unless we are certain they will be in a position to be economically self-sufficient. The Farm Credit Corporation will, like a bank, only lend money to someone who has more than enough collateral and good prospects.
The federal government must provide more money to allow for expansion. Many people have been writing to me complaining about this problem. I am sure I get a letter every week from someone who is not smart enough to realize that the federal government is not going to lend him money to go into farming. These letters say, "I was raised on a farm. My wife was raised on a farm. We moved into a city. We have been kicked around from job to job, from unemployment insurance office to unemployment insurance office, and now we want to go back and establish a farm. We know where there is a farm available for so many thousands of dollars which we believe would be suitable. We have talked to the people who have it and we think we could make a go of it. However, we have talked to the Farm Credit Corporation and to other lending agencies and they say no money is available for us to go into business."
Maybe these people would not make a go of it but, Mr. Speaker, they were raised on a farm and I say that those who have been raised on a farm have a pretty good idea of what farming is all about. They know you do not start at the top. They know you do not start with a registered herd of cattle in a nice big barn. They are well aware of the fact that it takes two generations, but they also are aware of the fact that if they work 15 or 16 hours a day and if the facilities are available
Problems of Farmers
and other criteria are met they have a good chance to make a living.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
These are the type of people who came to Ottawa today. They did not come here only as dairy farmers or grain producers; they came here as farmers. I think it is about time this government decided how they can help these people if they want to help them. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) is here. I believe he will remember that when he sat on the other side as minister of agriculture he had the idea-it certainly was an idea which I and many farmers across this country bought-that if we were to start a short range program this would not be satisfactory and that what we should have is a long term program which would meet the needs of the farm population and the industry involved. For this purpose we developed the program commonly known as ARDA.
I believe ARDA has accomplished many things. However, after listening to the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, who is responsible for ARDA, speak to the farmers a few hours ago I wondered whether he really had read what we wanted to do when we set up ARDA. The political patronage which is going on in respect of ARDA is not what it was set up for. It was set up to be a long range program for the benefit of agriculture. It was not set up to give patronage to a few people in a few counties who may be friends of a few members or members collectively. I believe this is part of the problem. Most of us look to ARDA as a means to end some of the problems.
I heard the minister stand up and say that we were going to end the problem of those in the Ottawa valley who are almost hillbillies. These are the people who live on rocky farms where they must farm between the rocks. This is all right when you have a team of oxen and a total production of four or five acres, but how can you drive a tractor around those rocks? It was said that these farms would be made into units which would grow trees instead of rocks and weeds. What happened? Nothing happened; they are still there.
We have had some good schemes. We developed a scheme in the interlake area of Manitoba which is the biggest patronage organization I have ever seen. The government of Manitoba loves the government now in power in Ottawa because they have spread patronage in the interlake area. This area is

May 24. 1967
Problems of Farmers
supposed to be a pattern, but if this is to be the pattern then I do not want anything to do with it. ARDA could be better than that. I understand there is not much difference between what has happened there and what has happened in the Lake St. John area. Do not forget that there were many farmers from the Lake St. John area here today. When they pound on the govenrment's door the government is too scared to let them in. These are not farmers from my area. They are farmers from the areas not far from the area of the minister who has done a great deal to stir them up. I believe there is something wrong with the government's attitude toward the farmer.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext: Why do you say that when there are farmers in the gallery?

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext: I do not know whether there are farmers in the gallery.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext: Do not say the government did not let them in. They were let in.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Maybe they did. I certainly do not wish to emphasize that point because it is not the po nt I am making. The point I am attempting to make is that they came because they want to know what is happening. ARDA may be much more important than what they are here for. ARDA was intended to bring about the solution of a number of problems. It was not our intention that under ARDA the provincial governments would be able to use the money for handouts in various areas. I had expected that the federal government would have control over it. Exactly the same thing has happened in the Department of Industry. The provincial government gets control of the money and uses it for handouts. This does not solve the problem on a national scale.
These people who are here today are interested in a solution on a national scale. If the government does not face up to the need for a solution to the agricultural problem, the day will come when it will be in serious difficulty. Some of these people live on farms in which they have a $50,000 investment. At the end of the year they have a net profit of $500 or $600. They legitimately and properly come to parliament now for a solution to their problem. If a person were to run any other kind of a business with a $45,000 or $50,000 investment and a similar return, obviously he would be out of business in a short time. None of his creditors would carry him for the 30 days necessary to get stock on the shelves.

This is the position in which we are placing the farmer.
We are lucky that for 20 years our farmers have been able to live off the depreciation wh.ch normally is allowed in a business. No farmers are putting away a depreciation allowance. I know people who live on farms and have never put anything back into those farms. I know this because I was in the second generation in that area. I know now, however, that farmers buy fertilizer by the carload because they find it is necessary to put back into the agricultural land some of the things which were taken out without any provision being made to replace them. It is difficult for them to do this with their current operating expenses.
It seems to me that the government should read some of the speeches which were made a few years ago. I can still remember the hon. member for Moose Jaw standing up in this house and telling the minister of agriculture of that day to get off his fat surplus and go out and sell wheat. I can remember when the government decided to do just that. They went to Poland, Czechoslovakia and finally to China. Eventually Russia came to us to buy wheat. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, I should say that I was not referring to the present member for Moose Jaw. I was referr ng to the member who preceded him, H.s Worship "Scoop" Lewry of that city. The fact is that the government sent out teams. The former minister of trade and commerce is remembered favourably by me because of the fact that he sent out teams to sell. They went out and sold. I really can see no difference between the situation then and the situation today in respect of the dairy industry and other farm commodities. This includes soybean producers, poultry producers, and others.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
We can produce in this country and if we are going to have economic farm units we must produce to capacity; otherwise there will not be people on these farms and they will be idle. If we produce to capacity we can outstrip our ability to consume and we must get out into world markets and sell our produce.
It is surprising that a country of this size is importing millions of pounds of cheese, in fact almost as much as we sell. It was interesting to note that at a cheese party to which I was invited the other day about 40 different kinds of cheese were being served but only three of them were made in Canada. The first,
May 24, 1967

which could be sold internationally, was Oka. The second was Canadian cheddar of various grades, medium, mild and old, and there were fancy cheeses produced by Black Diamond and Kraft.
The Department of Agriculture has done nothing about the fact that we are buying more cheese than we are exporting. Obviously it would be possible for us to manufacture Camembert and other types of cheeses that are imported, just as we have manufactured various types of wine. These cheeses may have different names but I am sure we could find markets for them just as we have found world markets for Canadian cheddar.
As the world population increases and the demand for more food grows I am sure we can produce more products. We will then be able to lend other countries the money to purchase our products just as we did in respect of our wheat sales to Poland and Czechoslovakia. We heard a great deal of outcry from various people about lending money to communist countries to purchase our products, but I wonder how many of those same people today would advocate a discontinuance of this practice. After lending these people this money through the international exchange fund we found that at the end of the stated term the product had been sold.
My grievance is not mine particularly because I have no cattle on my farm and I do not farm it. It is the grievance of the 20,000 people who came here today from the immediate area and the other 20,000 who did not come. The government will have to call a federal-provincial conference with the farm organizations in order to outline honestly to the farmers what they ought to do. This conference should listen to the problems of the farmers, although obviously the farmers are going to ask for more than they expect and will be told they will get less than we could give them. In any event we must solve their problems before they become acute.
The agricultural industry is the backbone of the very fabric of our economy. Agricultural problems cannot be solved by subsidies or stop-gap payments such as the $200 per farmer because these are only temporary measures. A long range program must be developed as quickly as possible. A serious investigation of the ARDA program must be undertaken by the committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development this year. If we are to develop a long range program as a solution to the agricultural problems faced by the farmers of Canada we must develop it on a different basis from our present programs.
Problems oj Farmers
The government must present a better image to the farmers of this country than the image presented to them this afternoon or it will never solve the problems. This will not only be to the detriment of the farmer but also to the detriment of the nation.
