speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like the hon. member to realize that we are perfectly aware of the crucial problem facing the farmers, and I should like to ask him whether he does not think that, in the past four years, the government has done a lot to improve the fate of the farmer?

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I do agree. Ever since I came here ten years ago the government has worked hard year by year to solve the immediate problems. The beauty of the ARDA program was that it was intended not only to provide stop-igap assistance to farmers but something that would be of future benefit to them. It was my hope that as a result we would be able to look ahead and see a much broader picture which would give some hope to those people who have been hanging on for so long in the hope that some beneficial change would be made in the field of agriculture.
It is my belief that the present Minister of Agriculture deserves a great deal of credit for setting up the manufacturing milk policy. This was a step in the right direction, but I think he will eventually find that he will be playing one farmer against another because he did not also establish a policy in respect of fluid and bulk milk. I am sure he will find in the long run that this neglect will prove disadvantageous to Canadian farmers. I am happy to agree that the present Minister of Agriculture has done his share in the stop-gap program, just as other ministers in other governments have done, but the farmers are not going to be satisfied with only stop-gap arrangements.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal first with-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Order, please. Does the hon. member for Qu'Appelle wish to comment on the same matter raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming?

May 24, 1967
Problems of Farmers

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The grievance raised by the hon. member for Timis-kaming can be dramatised by the fact that the farmers of Canada, who represent the most stable element in the population, have seen fit to leave their farms during the busy spring season to come here by the thousands to present their case to the government. Surely this is an indication that something serious is amiss.
I recall that during the first few weeks after I became minister of agriculture I made a national television broadcast pointing out to the people in the cities that if one compared agricultural income with that of any other segment of our society one would find that agricultural income was steadily declining, not only in relation to the working man, with whom the farmer should not be compared, but in relation to the independent businessman who has a similar type of investment and the same long hours of work. At that time I asked the people in the cities of Canada to give their blessing and backing to my efforts to get farm income moving upward in order to provide reasonable equity compared with other segments of industry in Canada. During the time I held the portfolio I tried to complete some basic agricultural reforms to which I intend to refer later.
In view of the difficulties faced in the last four years by the agricultural industry, resulting in part from the tremendous revolution in machinery and technology and capital investment, I have taken the position that this industry needs all the help it can get. I do not intend to bore the house with figures indicating the tremendous adjustments that have been made in the last few years by the farming industry in order to keep up with technology and mechanization, but I am going to say what I have wanted to say for the last four years but have kept quiet because of my reluctance to hinder the efforts of my successors in trying to bring some form of assistance to the agricultural industry in this country.
Let me now say what I have held in abeyance because I felt that any minister facing the tremendous difficulties involved should be given every opportunity to solve them. There has been talk in the house over the last four years about the necessity of a national farm policy. We have had policy studies, and now we have task forces. All these devices are delaying tactics which indicate to me that the government does not know what to do and does not know where it is going.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROBLEMS OF FARMERS
speechtext:
This is the essence of the difficulty. I do not think we need a study to tell the farmers and the people of Canada that our agricultural industry, as was stated by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), has reached a level of productive efficiency beyond the capacity of the domestic market of this country to absorb. It is as simple as that. Fortunately for those of us who come from the west we have an organization, the Canadian Wheat Board, through which we can channel this additional production because of increased productive efficiency and make it available in the markets of the world.
It is true that by using the traditional method of cash sales by the Canadian Wheat Board our exports were lower by 275 million bushels a year. When our government took on the responsibility of making credit sales and used the technique of the long term agreement with state run nations, mostly communist, when we made these two major businesslike approaches to the market exports climbed to the present level of approximately 600 million bushels a year and we could sell another 200 million bushels if we had the grain.
The interesting thing about these facts is that exactly seven years ago the farmers of western Canada were just as angry, just as frustrated, as are the farmers of eastern Canada today and those all across this country in the dairy industry. When I went to the farmers in 1960 and asked for their help and co-operation in backing me in a program of going out to sell their wheat abroad, asked them to give me time to demonstrate that it would be better for all of us if we sold our wheat abroad, and said that the maximum price would rise 50 cents a bushel when they were only asking for 20 cents more a bushel, the farmers gave me that breathing time. I think we demonstrated to the satisfaction of most people in western Canada-this area has never been traditionally Conservative in politics but when elections are held the people forget what the political names are and remember that ours was the first government in their living memory that ever tried to do something dramatic on their behalf-that we had the answers to some of these problems.
By staying together the farmers have developed a voice. In 1965, because of the incompetence of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and his failure to support them in that crisis, we saw the price of wheat drop 17 cents. The farmer was told he was selling so many bushels and making so
May 24, 1967



much money that he would not notice the drop of 17 cents a bushel. The farmer gave his answer on November 8, 1965, by cleaning out every Liberal in western Canada except one in the city of St. Boniface. I ask hon. members to look at a record of wheat prices since. Amazingly they started to climb back to the maximum the minute the farmers stuck together. Therefore I think the lesson of this march should be clear to the government.
I recall reading about and watching on television a similar march that took place in Quebec city a year ago. In the province of Quebec 10,000 farmers were trying to tell their story to the provincial government of that day. Not much was done to assist the farmers. Three months later the government of that province changed. That is what happens when farmers stick together. Forty-eight counties of Quebec saw to it that the government changed. I would remind the government that in their indifference in handling this delegation today and telling them they are coming here to strike against the public interest because what they are asking for would cost $90 million, and the government is busy with Viet Nam and the Middle East, they ignore the basic fact that there will be support by the people for a government only if there is no poverty and no injustice. And there is injustice in the income that the agricultural industry is receiving today. That is why the farmers are here.
The farmers who are here today on this march are not on the verge of extinction because of marginal land ownership. These farmers are not the ones who cannot adjust. These are the best farmers in Canada, led by the most responsible farm organizations in this country. Who has ever told this house that the U.C.C. is a radical, revolutionary group? Who has ever told this house that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is a radical, revolutionary group? These are the most stable groups in the body politic of Canada. They asked the farmers to come to Ottawa to add weight to the briefs they have presented to the government in the last four years, and the farmers have come here. This demonstrates the deep feeling among farmers in respect of their problems.
I am going to divert for a moment to point out what I think is an opportunity for the government to get out of this dilemma. I hold in my hand a pamphlet put out by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool entitled "Famine In The Future." It arrived this week in the mail of hon. members. I ask hon. members to read 27053-35J
Problems oj Farmers
this booklet and then they will see the answers to the problems of farmers in every industrial nation of the world, not only Canada. In this book we are told by the best mind in Canada today on agricultural policy, Dr. Menzies, that we have to face the facts, that by the end of this century we will have to feed approximately six billion people in the world.
The F.A.O. has pleaded with the nations of the industrial world to forget national differences, to forget their day to day problems and face the fact that today the nations of the world are facing a crisis. What do the nations of the world need? I can put it in two words-food and fibre. The F.A.O. in 1949 requested that greater effort be made in these fields. In 1959 it pleaded with the nations of the world to take action to solve these problems. The situation was so serious in 1964 that the F.A.O. issued a special report in which it asked for co-operation, and the answer it received from Canada was: We will set up a task force to study the matter.
It may be asked what this has to do with the debate we are holding today and the grievance we are discussing. It is a fact that we are not fighting communism in the world today. What we are fighting in the world today is poverty and injustice all over the world and not just in Canada. As the President of the United States told the American Congress, all the nations of the world must ask their producers to go full out and produce the food necessary to carry the world over the next 20 years and give our world institutions under the United Nations and through joint bilateral programs and so on a chance to build up the productive know-how because the next 20 years are the crisis years.
What do the people of the world want? They want proteins, proteins in milk, proteins in poultry products, proteins in red meats, proteins in soybeans. What nation is better prepared and more able to produce these things than Canada?
The dairy industry of Canada is frustrated today because of a surplus of 2 per cent milk. Because we can produce more milk than can be consumed in our cities the dairy farmer's price has been held down. What are the solutions to these problems? There are two solutions in my opinion. One is the short term solution of a subsidy to raise the price to that which will produce a bare living standard; otherwise all the investment in this very expensive industry will be lost. The other choice is to remember the salient fact that I brought out earlier, namely, why should there be a

May 24, 1967
Problems of Farmers
crisis in the dairy industry when the world desperately needs our proteins, when the world desperately wants skim milk powder and butter oil? Bring the two together and you reconstitute homogenized milk.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
We have the technology and the ability in Canada. All that is stopping us from curing this problem is the psychological block in the minds of the members on the front benches of the government. I recall meeting with the ten provincial agricultural ministers in 1961 and obtaining an agreement from them that the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec and the federal minister of agriculture would sit down together, forget partisan politics and do something to cure the problem facing the dairy industry. We agreed upon a plan.
At that time the government of Quebec was Liberal, the government of Ontario was Conservative and so was the federal government. We forgot that one government was Liberal and the others Conservative and we agreed upon a joint plan. That plan depended on Quebec passing legislation to give power to the farmers to form a single milk organization which would control the production and distribution of milk in Quebec and across the boundary in Ontario. Ontario had the necessary legislation but it had to persuade the various milk organizations in that province to accept the eventual liaison with Quebec, following which the federal government would take the surplus off the market and make sure that the price of milk would rise to such a level as to give the farmers a fair return without the necessity of a public subsidy. That was the simple, honest and straight forward plan which we accepted.
I do not hold it against the government of Mr. Lesage that he gave higher priorities to education, social welfare, hydro development and so on. However, the fact remains that his government did not introduce that legislation until the spring of 1966, and Ontario's efforts to bring its organizations together were thwarted until the Quebec government made the first move. The Quebec Liberal government fell in 1966 and another one took its place. Several weeks later the ministers of agriculture of Quebec and Ontario met in Montreal and agreed to come to the federal Minister of Agriculture and suggest to him to forget partisan politics and come together on the old agreement of 1961. What happened then? Somebody thought there should be a political battle between the federal Minister of Agriculture and the Ontario minister of

agriculture, and that is the reason the plan was not accepted. That is the reason for the farmer's march on Ottawa which is taking place today. The fact is that the government has marked time ever since and has decided upon subsidies, which the farmers know is no answer to the fundamental problem.
I can speak with some feeling on this subject. In 1958 I undertook a survey of the eastern half of my riding of Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan. I found that half the farmers had a cash income of less than $1,000 a year. Today when I go through those same areas I find that as a result of fundamentally sound agricultural policies the farmers who were getting less than $1,000 cash income have incomes of $6,000, $9,000 or $13,000 gross which gives them a net income of $1,000 or $2,000 a year. I saw a change in these people. Although they have to raise their families on $700 or $800 a year and their only chance to enjoy life is to go to a fair once a year, and although they are in debt up to their ears, they know they are doing something worth while, first, because at the present time they have enough money to meet the heavy debts incurred in the purchase of machinery, land and fertilizer and, second and above all, they know they are helping to feed the hungry people of the world.
I suggest that a parallel situation exists in Canada in the dairy industry and in the fishing and forest industries. The world is in desperate need of the products of these three industries. I think that the farmers, the lumbermen and the fishermen would not only feel happier if their pockets were a little fuller but also if they knew they were helping to meet the great challenge of our day, namely, the famine which faces the world. I think this is both the long range and the immediate solution.
A moment ago I mentioned the need for fibre, lumber and newsprint. The hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned reforestation. I recall that in 1962 and again in 1963 I proposed, on behalf of the government of that day, that we should take 20 million acres of abandoned farms in eastern Canada and spend on them $2 billion during a ten-year period to develop a commercial type of wood. The farmers in those marginal areas would have benefited from 90 per cent of the $2 billion which would have been spent on labour in the planting of and looking after trees. This would have been tied up with the expansion of the beef industry, so that the income of the people in these areas would
May 24. 1987

have been given a boost. I am speaking of the Bruce peninsula, the clay belt, the Ottawa valley, Lac Saint-Jean, and right down through Gaspe and the maritimes.
The proposal to spend $2 billion to reforest 20 million acres was described by the Prime Minister of this country as a policy for dogs. He visualized dogs being very happy with all those trees. That was all that his wisecracking mind could see. He did not even know that to spend $2 billion on this type of project would not only produce an income which would carry these people over the intervening years when the trees would be growing but that in 35 years time they would be worth a minimum of $12 billion and, with present prices, more likely $24 billion. Whenever a government can spend $2 billion which will produce $24 billion a generation later, that is a good expenditure. A capital value of $12 billion to $24 billion added to the beef and the recreational industries of these areas, would have meant an increase in income of at least $600 million to $700 million a year. It would also provide us with the foreign exchange which this country so desperately needs. But above all it would make thousands of farmers know that they were needed not only in Canada but in the whole world. They would feel satisfaction in that as they helped to raise their own incomes they were helping to feed, clothe and provide shelter for the people of this world.
That program has never been mentioned by the government in the house since it took office. Apparently they still think of it as a policy for dogs. A farmer does not care what he grows, whether it be dairy cows, beef cattle or trees, as long as the income from his acres is giving his family a livelihood and the possibility to raise his children in dignity. This is what I hold against the present government.
I mentioned earlier that by being united the farmers can achieve much more than if they divide into various groups. I mentioned the case of the 10,000 farmers who marched on Quebec city last year. I mentioned the fact that as a result of their march they went back to their counties and brought changes to the rural areas in Quebec which brought about a change in government. I also gave the example of how the western farmers, after 40 years of fighting each other, learned to work and vote together. I will give one more example because we in Canada are not alone in facing these problems. The same surplus of dairy products exists in the United States. Our surplus is 2 per cent while the surplus in
Problems of Farmers
the United States is 3 per cent. The reasons for the surplus are the same in both countries. The companies in both countries which buy the dairy products from the farmers are more disposed to sell them in the cities. It never enters their mind that the people of Formosa, Japan, Korea, Hong Kong and Indonesia want what the farmer is producing here. They continue the routine of selling to the cities. The companies in both countries are equally guilty.
While speaking on the question of farm activity in the United States, I would suggest that hon. members take a look at Hansard of last February or March where they will find the debate on the estimates of the former minister of trade and commerce. At that time I told him that if he was not going to act with regard to world wheat prices I would. I asked the farm leaders in western Canada to approach the farm leaders of the United States and to suggest to them that we should all stand together in trying to get the United States government to change its mind on wheat prices.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I have given public credit, and I do so now in this house, to Mr. Gibbings of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Mr. Atkins of the National Farm Union and Mr. Runciman, who made these contacts with their counterparts. I went down and met the farm leaders of the United States in the office of the secretary of agriculture in Washington. I told them what I was going to do. The farmers asked the government of the United States to change its attitude on wheat prices but the government refused. The farmers gave them their answer in November last by cleaning out 23 of the 24 Democrats in the farm areas.
My point, therefore, to the farmers who are gathered here today is that although you only comprise 10 per cent of the population of Canada, which is far from the days when the figure was 30 or 50 per cent, if that 10 per cent learn the lessons of the last few years and stick together, not only in the west but in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes, they can achieve the same result as the United States farmers achieved last year when they forced the government of that country to change its attitude on world wheat prices.
Agriculture is a basic industry but we have to get across the idea in the cities that unless agriculture is prosperous Canada is not prosperous. It seems odd that we should have to learn this lesson the hard way. You will recall that when the tremendous wheat sales took

May 24, 1967
Problems of Farmers
place in 1961 they coincided with the movement of the economic barometer for every industry in this country. Within weeks the hard industries, such as farm machinery and trucks, moved up. Within months the steel industry and the mining industry began to move up. Employment moved up and wages moved up. There is an immediate reaction upon industry that serves the Canadian people when agriculture is prosperous. If there is an upsurge in manufacturing it takes two or three years before the results are felt by agriculture. However, when those engaged in agriculture get any money the results are felt immediately in the whole economic community. This fact has been admitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) in the present government and by the head of the Bank of Canada. Everyone accepts this principle. However, the government is failing to put it into practice. The health of agriculture is basic to the health of the country. That fact can be demonstrated to your heart's content.
It seems odd that in China today this subject is being debated. The cadres want to industrialize very rapidly but the government says no, we have to build up our farm industry. A great debate is going on because the Chinese government learned in 1959, 1960 and 1961 that if you let your agricultural industry drop, as they did when they moved the labour battalions to the cities to build the schools and roads they needed, then the whole economy almost collapses. They have had to go back and do it the hard way. Do we in Canada have to learn that lesson? We have to remember at all times that the agricultural industry, even if only 10 per cent of the population is engaged in that industry, must be kept not only to feed our own people but to help in the task of feeding people all over the world. It is for this reason agriculture must be basic.
I should have liked to continue and explain the principles of ARDA as a long range approach to the problems of the marginal farmer. This program is designed to help him with his difficulties and enable him to take advantage of all these opportunities. I would have liked to talk about changes that should be made in the Agricultural Stabilization Act, the Farm Credit Act and the Crop Insurance Act.
I should like to remind the government that in the committee on agriculture and colonization in 1963 and 1964 members of every political party, Liberal, Conservative, N.D.P. and so on, agreed upon a fundamental program to help the eastern fanner in connection

with feed grains. We sat here all that year and waited. When the legislation came before us we found that the government had apparently ignored the basic conclusions upon which all parties had agreed in a quiet, constructive committee. I mention these things because it grieves me terribly to recall that the proposed feed grain assistance act which I introduced in the house in 1963 never saw the light of day. It was to be one of the basic pieces of legislation, along with ARDA, which would give eastern farmers the same uplift the farmers of western Canada had received. So the eastern farmer has waited all these years since 1963 and all he has received is talk. He has never had action.
I do not intend to criticize the principles of ARDA. I believe they are essentially sound. But I feel the minister has been more concerned about politics in the province of Quebec than he has been with using that legislation to do what it was primarily designed to do. The legislation was designed to get the local people, businessmen, professional people and farmers, to forget partisan politics and work together to raise the income level of the community. If the program has become a means of pouring money into an area in the form of subsidies, studies or surveys without the fundamental participation of the people in their own future, then I say that the government has destroyed or seriously hurt a very sound bit of legislation.
I could go on indefinitely. However, I believe I have said enough to indicate that the problems of the marginal farmer are still with us. Every time I look at the figures and realize that 83 per cent of the farmers of Quebec are below the minimum standard of a modern industrial state, that 87 per cent of the farmers in the maritimes are below this standard and 60 per cent of the farmers across the country are below the standard, I realize that the problems of the marginal farmer are still with us. When you are the author of legislation you naturally feel that your child is being neglected, and you hate to see this.
I know the minister made a tremendous effort, after waiting a year with no action, to learn how this legislation operated. I know his civil servants made an effort to get the program started. What I do know now is that the very dreams we built together are disappearing because the people see no hope and the minister spends all his time on politics and none on the problems of these marginal farmers. Our problem today, as I say, is not fighting communism. Our problem today is
May 24, 1967	COMMONS
fighting poverty by self-help rather than handouts. Our problem today is to fight injustice by doing those things that give people hope there will be some answer to their problems.
I do not pretend, Mr. Speaker, that all the problems were solved when I was minister or that they will all be solved in the future. However, I do know that an honest effort was made, and I hate to see us marking time. I hate to see this pre-occupation with things as far reaching as the Middle East or Viet Nam because the root problem is the same. If we were more concerned in Viet Nam with the division of land between the landlords and the peasant, I believe an answer would come more quickly. However, with the world appealing to us for help, with the FAO asking for help, the people of our generation in Canada must ask if we are going to be able to meet these requests. I want to be able to meet this challenge in my generation, not by handouts at home or by handouts abroad but by the adoption of the principle of self-help.
